newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's top "wise man" calls for EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's top "wise man" calls for EMU delay.

text.p: Doubts that Germany will make the grade for European monetary union gained new force on Saturday when a top government advisor called for a delay and a leading research institute cut its growth forecast.
Herbert Hax, head of the "five wise men" economic advisory panel, said Germany would in all likelihood miss the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit and public debt goals this year.
And, in one of the most forthright calls by a senior German advisor to date, Hax said Bonn should put off joining the euro currency project until its own financial house is in order.
"The truth is quite simple: Stability comes before the timetable," Hax told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has pledged to cut the budget deficit this year to below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Meeting the goal would enable European Union leaders to give Germany the green light next year to take part in the scheduled start of EMU in 1999. Hax said that would be tough.
"The government forecast is 2.9 percent, but there are others who predict over three percent," he told Bild am Sonntag in remarks released in advance of the paper's Sunday edition.
"If you take the stability criteria seriously, Germany will probably not be able to introduce the euro as planned in 1999."
He also said Germany would probably overstep the EMU public debt target of 60 percent of GDP in 1997.
A Finance Ministry spokesman rejected the comments by Hax, who he said had unfairly prejudged the chances of Germany and other EU states joining EMU with the year barely a quarter old.
"Herr Hax...is starting a debate which shouldn't be taking place and which hinders fiscal consolidation. There is no reason to abandon the government's policy," he told Reuters.

Hax's comments carry weight because the forecasts of the politically-independent wise men underpin government budget planning. The group last November forecast a deficit this year of 3.3 percent of GDP, down from a final 3.8 percent in 1996.

Waigel's budget assumes economic growth of 2.5 percent -- but that forecast received a blow on Saturday after another of Germany's top-ranking economic research groups knocked a half-point off its GDP growth forecast to two percent.

The news magazine Focus said the Halle-based IWH institute had cut its economic forecast because of the German economy's stagnation in the final quarter of 1996. The IWH forecast an jobless rate for 1997 of 11 percent -- equivalent to over 4.2 million -- up from its previous outlook of 10.4 percent.
The IWH is the second top think-tank to cut its growth forecast to two percent, but a third, the Kiel-based IfW institute said it expected the government growth forecast to be met.
That will not be enough, however, to reduce the 1997 budget deficit, which the IfW forecast at 3.5 percent of GDP.
Although dole queues are expected to shorten during the spring, lower tax revenues and extra jobless benefit costs are already tipping the fiscal arithmetic against Waigel.
Hax said Germany and the EU must make it clear now whether they intend to make use of the leeway offered by Maastricht or to put off EMU until state finances are in better shape.

"Either you loosen the criteria, and you have to say so now, or Germany will have to get ready for the euro later," he said. "Unfortunately, the politicians have turned the possibility of a delay into a taboo."
He added: "Germany and a group of other countries will probably not fulfill the convergence criteria before 1998. Only after that can the euro be introduced in all these countries."
That would mean that the euro would be launched in 2000. "That would be better than if four or five countries march ahead," Hax said.
